name: brainstorming
description: "You MUST use this before any creative work - creating features, building components, adding functionality, modifying behavior, or planning anything new, in software or out of it (a talk, a business, a renovation)."
---

# Brainstorming

You are very good at building. You build what you believe your human
partner wants, and that belief is usually thinner than it feels. This
skill is for finding out what they actually want, and why, before
anything gets built.

People often haven't finished working out what they want. Good questions
help them think it through. When you understand the why, you make the
hundred decisions they never mention the way they would have made them.

## First: What Do You Actually Know?

Before you reply, ask yourself: what do I know about what they want, and
why?

- **Everything that matters is in the request** ("make the icon cornflower
  blue"). This is a quick, clear task. Do it, and say what you did.
- **Something non-trivial is missing.** Start the conversation.

## Your First Message

Your first message is two things, in this order:

1. One line letting them know that if they'd rather skip the questions and
   have you just start, they can say so. If they take you up on it, this
   skill is done: state any significant how-it-gets-made choice
   (platform, language, medium) in one plain line, then do what they
   asked through the normal workflow.
2. One open question that gets them describing. Ask about a real moment
   or a concrete picture: "What's the moment you find yourself wishing
   this existed?" or "Tell me about the people who'll be in the room."

That's the whole message.

## The Conversation

Each message ends with one question: a single sentence with no list of
example answers hanging off it. Use plain language, pitched just a little
above where your human partner is. Match their vocabulary; never use
process jargon.

Be clear and concise. Lead with what matters. Avoid jargon. When you
report what you found, give them the most important findings and offer
the rest.

**Get them describing.** Open questions come first. Their own words carry
intent that your options can't. Offer a short menu only when they're
stuck. When they say "just guess" or "what do you think?", propose
something concrete.

**How it gets made.** Every project rests on choices about medium, tools,
materials, and resources: the platform, programming language, and
libraries for an app; the medium for a piece of art. Find out early which
of those choices they want to make, which they're handing to you, and what
they already have to work with. Someone with strong views or skills will
want to talk it through. Someone counting on you needs sensible defaults,
said in plain words. When there's existing work, build on what it already
uses. Any choice you make goes in the design as your call, never as
something they agreed to.

**Ground to cover.** This is territory, not a script. Never read these
out as questions:

- what kind of thing this is, and what makes it special
- why now, and what success looks like to them
- goals, non-goals, and anti-goals (what would make this a failure even
  if it technically works)
- prior art: what they've seen elsewhere, loved or hated
- current state: what exists now, what they've tried
- the details they care about

**Questions that work** anchor in specifics: "Walk me through the last
time...", "If it could only do one of these well, which?", "What would
make you wince if I got it wrong?" A guess they can correct ("I'm
guessing this is because X keeps biting you?") often beats a question.

**Offer recon.** Once you have a bit of grounding and looking would help,
offer to go look: their codebase or project, their own files and data,
or the web. Say what you'd look for. They decide whether you go.

**Think wide privately.** Before you propose anything, come up with
several ideas and drop the weak ones, including any that fight what
they've told you about why. Show the comparison only when it helps them
decide.

**Show, don't tell.** Offer the visual companion (below) whenever seeing
would help more than reading:

- something they'll look at: a screen, a page, a printout, a sign
- a layout or arrangement: of a screen, a room, a schedule
- a flow or a sequence of steps
- options that would look different from each other
- a structure that's easier to see than read: a diagram, a timeline, a map

Once they've accepted, use it for mockups to react to, side-by-side
options, and throwaway prototypes they can click.

**Spike to feel things out.** Agentic work is waterfall, but very, very
fast. A quick throwaway build is often the cheapest way to learn what
they want or whether something works. Offer one when it would help.
When they just want to spike, get out of the way. Spikes get no tests
or minimal ones, aren't bulletproof, and skip the plan, implementation,
and review process. Bring what the spike taught you back into the
conversation.

## Play It Back

Play back as you go. As soon as you understand one part well enough to
describe it (what it's for and who it serves, say, or how one piece
behaves), describe that part back in about 200-300 words, then return to
questions about the next part. Playback and questions alternate through
the whole conversation; the last chunk covers whatever is left.

Mark anything you're guessing as your guess; only what they said goes in
as theirs. End each chunk by asking what's wrong or missing.

Before you send a chunk, check it: does it describe something they'll
look at, like a page, a screen, a schedule, or a printout? If so, and
they haven't seen the visual companion offer yet, send the offer instead
(its own message, below) and hold the chunk for the next message. Once
they've accepted, put a mockup next to the description.

## Size the Work

Once you understand what they want, pick a size and say it in plain
words. They can override it.

| Size | The full description | Then |
|------|----------------------|------|
| A quick, clear task | the request itself | do it |
| A small change | in chat | build it through the normal workflow |
| A project with a written design | a written design document | a full plan (for software: superpowers:writing-plans) |

If it grows mid-task, stop, say so, and step up a size.

If this is really several independent projects, say so, agree on an
order, and brainstorm them one at a time.

## The Written Design

For a project, write a plain document a talented builder in the domain
could plan from without going back to your human partner. Cover:

- intent and the why
- goals, non-goals, anti-goals
- constraints
- the parts of the how they decided, as they decided them
- what's left to the builder

**Where it goes:** in a software repo,
`docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`, committed.
Otherwise, ask. Your human partner's preferences override both.

**Builder check:** dispatch a fresh subagent with
`builder-check-prompt.md` in this directory. When you tell your human
partner you're writing it up, say a reviewer will read it first and you
may come back once with a few questions. Don't hand over the document
until the check is back. Sort what the builder asks into three piles:

- **Answered already** by the conversation or the project: put the answer
  in the document.
- **Minor:** a sensible builder could settle it without changing what gets
  built. Settle it yourself and mark it in the document as your call.
- **Theirs:** only your human partner can answer it, and the answer changes
  what gets built.

Bring the "theirs" pile in one message, most important first. Update the
document with their answers, then hand it over with a short list of the
calls you made so they can check those while reading. That's the only
round of questions the check produces. Without a subagent tool, read the
document as that builder yourself.

<HARD-GATE>
Nothing gets built until your human partner approves the full
description: in chat for a small change, the document for a project.
Building includes writing product code, scaffolding, installing
dependencies, creating projects, and invoking an implementation skill.
Reading and exploring are fine.

Two exceptions. If they opted out of the questions, the skill is done
and the gate goes with it. A spike they said yes to may be built; it
stays labeled throwaway, and keeping what it produced is a new request
that comes back through this gate.

After a project's document is approved, the next step is the plan. For
software, invoke superpowers:writing-plans and no other skill.
</HARD-GATE>

## Red Flags

| Thought | Reality |
|---------|---------|
| "I'll offer options to save them effort" | Options steer. Ask them to describe it first. |
| "I'll fill in sensible defaults" | Good. Say them out loud. A default they never heard is one they couldn't reject. |
| "I should explain the process first" | Ask your question. The process shows itself. |
| "They said 'sounds good' to the idea" | Approval covers what you showed them. A description you haven't written isn't approved. |
| "The spike works, I'll keep building on it" | Keeping it is a new request. Back through the gate. |

## Visual Companion

A browser tab for showing mockups, diagrams, and prototypes. It's a
tool, not a mode: accepting it doesn't send every question to the
browser.

**Offer it just-in-time.** Offer it the first time one of the moments
above comes up, never upfront. The offer is its own message with nothing
else in it:

> "This might be easier if I show you. Want me to open a browser tab with some mockups?"

If they decline, stay in text and don't offer again unless they raise it.

**Per question, ask: would they understand this better by seeing it?**
Mockups, layouts, diagrams, and side-by-side designs go in the browser.
Requirements, scope, tradeoffs, and conceptual choices stay in text. A
question about a UI topic isn't automatically a visual question.

If they accept, read `visual-companion.md` in this directory before
starting the server.

5: 
6: # Systematic Debugging
7: 
8: ## Overview
9: 
10: **Core principle:** ALWAYS find root cause before attempting fixes. Symptom fixes are failure.
11: 
12: **Violating the letter of this process is violating the spirit of debugging.**
13: 
14: ## The Iron Law
15: 
16: ```
17: NO FIXES WITHOUT ROOT CAUSE INVESTIGATION FIRST
18: ```
19: 
20: If you haven't completed Phase 1, you cannot propose fixes.
21: 
22: ## When to Use
23: 
24: Use for ANY technical issue:
25: - Test failures
26: - Bugs in production
27: - Unexpected behavior
28: - Performance problems
29: - Build failures
30: - Integration issues
31: 
32: **Use this ESPECIALLY when:**
33: - Under time pressure (emergencies make guessing tempting)
34: - "Just one quick fix" seems obvious
35: - You've already tried multiple fixes
36: - Previous fix didn't work
37: - You don't fully understand the issue
38: 
39: **Don't skip when:**
40: - Issue seems simple (simple bugs have root causes too)
41: - You're in a hurry (rushing guarantees rework)
42: - Manager wants it fixed NOW (systematic is faster than thrashing)
43: 
44: ## The Four Phases
45: 
46: You MUST complete each phase before proceeding to the next.
47: 
48: ### Phase 1: Root Cause Investigation
49: 
50: **BEFORE attempting ANY fix:**
51: 
52: 1. **Read Error Messages Carefully**
53:    - Don't skip past errors or warnings
54:    - They often contain the exact solution
55:    - Read stack traces completely
56:    - Note line numbers, file paths, error codes
57: 
58: 2. **Reproduce Consistently**
59:    - Can you trigger it reliably?
60:    - What are the exact steps?
61:    - Does it happen every time?
62:    - If not reproducible → gather more data, don't guess
63: 
64: 3. **Check Recent Changes**
65:    - What changed that could cause this?
66:    - Git diff, recent commits
67:    - New dependencies, config changes
68:    - Environmental differences
69: 
70: 4. **Gather Evidence in Multi-Component Systems**
71: 
72:    **WHEN system has multiple components (CI → build → signing, API → service → database):**
73: 
74:    **BEFORE proposing fixes, add diagnostic instrumentation:**
75:    ```
76:    For EACH component boundary:
77:      - Log what data enters component
78:      - Log what data exits component
79:      - Verify environment/config propagation
80:      - Check state at each layer
81: 
82:    Run once to gather evidence showing WHERE it breaks
83:    THEN analyze evidence to identify failing component
84:    THEN investigate that specific component
85:    ```
86: 
87:    **Example (multi-layer system):**
88:    ```bash
89:    # Layer 1: Workflow
90:    echo "=== Secrets available in workflow: ==="
91:    echo "IDENTITY: $([ -n "${IDENTITY:-}" ] && echo SET || echo UNSET)"
92: 
93:    # Layer 2: Build script
94:    echo "=== Env vars in build script: ==="
95:    printenv IDENTITY >/dev/null 2>&1 && echo "IDENTITY in environment" || echo "IDENTITY not in environment"
96:

---
name: systematic-debugging
description: Use when encountering any bug, test failure, or unexpected behavior, before proposing fixes
---

# Systematic Debugging

## Overview

**Core principle:** ALWAYS find root cause before attempting fixes. Symptom fixes are failure.

**Violating the letter of this process is violating the spirit of debugging.**

## The Iron Law

```
NO FIXES WITHOUT ROOT CAUSE INVESTIGATION FIRST
```

If you haven't completed Phase 1, you cannot propose fixes.

## When to Use

Use for ANY technical issue:
- Test failures
- Bugs in production
- Unexpected behavior
- Performance problems
- Build failures
- Integration issues

**Use this ESPECIALLY when:**
- Under time pressure (emergencies make guessing tempting)
- "Just one quick fix" seems obvious
- You've already tried multiple fixes
- Previous fix didn't work
- You don't fully understand the issue

**Don't skip when:**
- Issue seems simple (simple bugs have root causes too)
- You're in a hurry (rushing guarantees rework)
- Manager wants it fixed NOW (systematic is faster than thrashing)

## The Four Phases

You MUST complete each phase before proceeding to the next.

### Phase 1: Root Cause Investigation

**BEFORE attempting ANY fix:**

1. **Read Error Messages Carefully**
   - Don't skip past errors or warnings
   - They often contain the exact solution
   - Read stack traces completely
   - Note line numbers, file paths, error codes

2. **Reproduce Consistently**
   - Can you trigger it reliably?
   - What are the exact steps?
   - Does it happen every time?
   - If not reproducible → gather more data, don't guess

3. **Check Recent Changes**
   - What changed that could cause this?
   - Git diff, recent commits
   - New dependencies, config changes
   - Environmental differences

4. **Gather Evidence in Multi-Component Systems**

   **WHEN system has multiple components (CI → build → signing, API → service → database):**

   **BEFORE proposing fixes, add diagnostic instrumentation:**
   ```
   For EACH component boundary:
     - Log what data enters component
     - Log what data exits component
     - Verify environment/config propagation
     - Check state at each layer

   Run once to gather evidence showing WHERE it breaks
   THEN analyze evidence to identify failing component
   THEN investigate that specific component
   ```

   **Example (multi-layer system):**
   ```bash
   # Layer 1: Workflow
   echo "=== Secrets available in workflow: ==="
   echo "IDENTITY: $([ -n "${IDENTITY:-}" ] && echo SET || echo UNSET)"

   # Layer 2: Build script
   echo "=== Env vars in build script: ==="
   printenv IDENTITY >/dev/null 2>&1 && echo "IDENTITY in environment" || echo "IDENTITY not in environment"

   # Layer 3: Signing script
   echo "=== Keychain state: ==="
   security list-keychains
   security find-identity -v

   # Layer 4: Actual signing
   codesign --sign "$IDENTITY" --verbose=4 "$APP"
   ```

   **This reveals:** Which layer fails (secrets → workflow ✓, workflow → build ✗)

5. **Trace Data Flow**

   **WHEN error is deep in call stack:**

   See `root-cause-tracing.md` in this directory for the complete backward tracing technique.

   **Quick version:**
   - Where does bad value originate?
   - What called this with bad value?
   - Keep tracing up until you find the source
   - Fix at source, not at symptom

### Phase 2: Pattern Analysis

**Find the pattern before fixing:**

1. **Find Working Examples**
   - Locate similar working code in same codebase
   - What works that's similar to what's broken?

2. **Compare Against References**
   - If implementing pattern, read reference implementation COMPLETELY
   - Don't skim - read every line
   - Understand the pattern fully before applying

3. **Identify Differences**
   - What's different between working and broken?
   - List every difference, however small
   - Don't assume "that can't matter"

4. **Understand Dependencies**
   - What other components does this need?
   - What settings, config, environment?
   - What assumptions does it make?

### Phase 3: Hypothesis and Testing

**Scientific method:**

1. **Form Single Hypothesis**
   - State clearly: "I think X is the root cause because Y"
   - Write it down
   - Be specific, not vague

2. **Test Minimally**
   - Make the SMALLEST possible change to test hypothesis
   - One variable at a time
   - Don't fix multiple things at once

3. **Verify Before Continuing**
   - Did it work? Yes → Phase 4
   - Didn't work? Form NEW hypothesis
   - DON'T add more fixes on top

4. **When You Don't Know**
   - Say "I don't understand X"
   - Don't pretend to know
   - Ask for help
   - Research more

### Phase 4: Implementation

**Fix the root cause, not the symptom:**

1. **Create Failing Test Case**
   - Simplest possible reproduction
   - Automated test if possible
   - One-off test script if no framework
   - MUST have before fixing
   - Use the `superpowers:test-driven-development` skill for writing proper failing tests

2. **Implement Single Fix**
   - Address the root cause identified
   - ONE change at a time
   - No "while I'm here" improvements
   - No bundled refactoring

3. **Verify Fix**
   - Test passes now?
   - No other tests broken?
   - Issue actually resolved?
   - Use the `superpowers:verification-before-completion` skill before claiming success

4. **If Fix Doesn't Work**
   - STOP
   - Count: How many fixes have you tried?
   - If < 3: Return to Phase 1, re-analyze with new information
   - **If ≥ 3: STOP and question the architecture (step 5 below)**
   - DON'T attempt Fix #4 without architectural discussion

5. **If 3+ Fixes Failed: Question Architecture**

   **Pattern indicating architectural problem:**
   - Each fix reveals new shared state/coupling/problem in different place
   - Fixes require "massive refactoring" to implement
   - Each fix creates new symptoms elsewhere

   **STOP and question fundamentals:**
   - Is this pattern fundamentally sound?
   - Are we "sticking with it through sheer inertia"?
   - Should we refactor architecture vs. continue fixing symptoms?

   **Discuss with your human partner before attempting more fixes**

   This is NOT a failed hypothesis - this is a wrong architecture.

## Red Flags - STOP and Follow Process

If you catch yourself thinking:
- "Quick fix for now, investigate later"
- "Just try changing X and see if it works"
- "Add multiple changes, run tests"
- "Skip the test, I'll manually verify"
- "It's probably X, let me fix that"
- "I don't fully understand but this might work"
- "Pattern says X but I'll adapt it differently"
- "Here are the main problems: [lists fixes without investigation]"
- Proposing solutions before tracing data flow
- **"One more fix attempt" (when already tried 2+)**
- **Each fix reveals new problem in different place**

**ALL of these mean: STOP. Return to Phase 1.**

**If 3+ fixes failed:** Question the architecture (see Phase 4.5)

## your human partner's Signals You're Doing It Wrong

**Watch for these redirections:**
- "Is that not happening?" - You assumed without verifying
- "Will it show us...?" - You should have added evidence gathering
- "Stop guessing" - You're proposing fixes without understanding
- "Ultra-think this" - Question fundamentals, not just symptoms
- "We're stuck?" (frustrated) - Your approach isn't working

**When you see these:** STOP. Return to Phase 1.

## Common Rationalizations

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "Issue is simple, don't need process" | Simple issues have root causes too. Process is fast for simple bugs. |
| "Emergency, no time for process" | Systematic debugging is FASTER than guess-and-check thrashing. |
| "Just try this first, then investigate" | First fix sets the pattern. Do it right from the start. |
| "I'll write test after confirming fix works" | Untested fixes don't stick. Test first proves it. |
| "Multiple fixes at once saves time" | Can't isolate what worked. Causes new bugs. |
| "Reference too long, I'll adapt the pattern" | Partial understanding guarantees bugs. Read it completely. |
| "I see the problem, let me fix it" | Seeing symptoms ≠ understanding root cause. |
| "One more fix attempt" (after 2+ failures) | 3+ failures = architectural problem. Question pattern, don't fix again. |

## Quick Reference

| Phase | Key Activities | Success Criteria |
|-------|---------------|------------------|
| **1. Root Cause** | Read errors, reproduce, check changes, gather evidence | Understand WHAT and WHY |
| **2. Pattern** | Find working examples, compare | Identify differences |
| **3. Hypothesis** | Form theory, test minimally | Confirmed or new hypothesis |
| **4. Implementation** | Create test, fix, verify | Bug resolved, tests pass |

## When Process Reveals "No Root Cause"

If systematic investigation reveals issue is truly environmental, timing-dependent, or external:

1. You've completed the process
2. Document what you investigated
3. Implement appropriate handling (retry, timeout, error message)
4. Add monitoring/logging for future investigation

**But:** 95% of "no root cause" cases are incomplete investigation.

## Supporting Techniques

These techniques are part of systematic debugging and available in this directory:

- **`root-cause-tracing.md`** - Trace bugs backward through call stack to find original trigger
- **`defense-in-depth.md`** - Add validation at multiple layers after finding root cause
- **`condition-based-waiting.md`** - Replace arbitrary timeouts with condition polling

# Agentic ODI [![Open the Living Studio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Open%20the%20Living%20Studio-F38020?style=for-the-badge&logo=cloudflare&logoColor=white)](https://agentic-odi.alehar.workers.dev/) [![CI](https://github.com/alehar9320/agentic-odi/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/alehar9320/agentic-odi/actions/workflows/ci.yml) [![codecov](https://codecov.io/gh/alehar9320/agentic-odi/branch/main/graph/badge.svg)](https://codecov.io/gh/alehar9320/agentic-odi) [![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/python-3.10%2B-blue.svg)](https://www.python.org/downloads/) [![uv](https://img.shields.io/badge/uv-managed-green)](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) [![Ruff](https://img.shields.io/endpoint?url=https://raw.githubusercontent.com/astral-sh/ruff/main/assets/badge/v2.json)](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff) [![FastMCP](https://img.shields.io/badge/FastMCP-powered-orange)](https://github.com/jlowin/fastmcp) [![pytest](https://img.shields.io/badge/tests-pytest-blue)](https://pytest.org) [![MCP](https://img.shields.io/badge/Model%20Context%20Protocol-enabled-8A2BE2)](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) > **[![Experimental](https://img.shields.io/badge/Experimental-1e293b?style=for-the-badge)](https://github.com/alehar9320/agentic-odi)** > **Experimental test to learn and evaluate the feasibility of utilizing Model Context Protocol (MCP) for Outcome-Driven Innovation (ODI) specifications.**
--- > **See it live:** **[agentic-odi.alehar.workers.dev](https://agentic-odi.alehar.workers.dev/)**. > No install required; the interface loads immediately, while live data, chat, and > mutations need the local sidecar ([Deployment](docs/deployment.md)). To run the > full stack yourself, jump to [Quick Start](#quick-start). **Agentic ODI** explores how the [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) can turn [Outcome-Driven Innovation](https://strategyn.com/outcome-driven-innovation/) into a live, agent-queryable source of context. Instead of feeding LLMs disconnected prompts, an MCP-powered ODI server acts as the "brain" of customer needs — letting agents invent, evaluate, and ideate solutions anchored in verified, measurable customer outcomes (Job Maps, Desired Outcomes, and Opportunity Scores). This repository is an experimental testbed for understanding server–client MCP communication streams, built on [`FastMCP`](https://github.com/jlowin/fastmcp). We don't publish dates. This page changes when the code does. **Project site:** the site lives at **[alehar9320.github.io/agentic-odi](https://alehar9320.github.io/agentic-odi/)**, with a documentation hub at **[alehar9320.github.io/agentic-odi/docs/](https://alehar9320.github.io/agentic-odi/docs/)**. It is republished by the `Pages` workflow on every push to `main`. The site is generated from this repository — the MCP tool reference, the connector catalog, the CLI tree, and the ODI schema are read from the code that ships, so they cannot drift from it. **Hosted Studio:** the experimental Living Studio UI runs at **[agentic-odi.alehar.workers.dev](https://agentic-odi.alehar.workers.dev/)**. It loads without a backend; live data needs the sidecar tunnel described in [Deployment](docs/deployment.md). Pull requests get preview URLs from Cloudflare Workers Builds. ## Code Overview A [uv workspace](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/concepts/projects/workspaces/) with shared tooling at the root. Packages live in `packages/`, runnable services in `apps/`, and deployment assets in `infra/`: | Path | Distribution | Description | |---|---|---| | **`packages/core/`** | `agentic-odi-core` | Domain models, the `ODIService` business-logic layer, repository implementations (in-memory and SQLite), the shared MCP tool contract, and ODI opportunity-score computation. | | **`packages/connectors/`** | `agentic-odi-connectors` | Pluggable MCP and REST connectors with presets and an ingest sink. | | **`apps/mcp-server/`** | `agentic-odi-mcp-server` | FastMCP server exposing Jobs, Steps, Desired Outcomes, Customer Outcomes, Evidence, and context tools over HTTP. Persists to SQLite by default. | | **`apps/studio-api/`** | `agentic-odi-studio-api` | FastAPI **Living Studio sidecar**. Serves config, health, canvas data, local mutations, MCP passthrough, SSE chat, conversation history, and the PM memory store, plus the built SPA. | | **`apps/cli/`** | `agentic-odi-cli` | Typer CLI with interactive chat plus full entity CRUD, `schema`, `connectors`, and local-first (`--backend local`) or remote (`--backend mcp`) data access. | | **`apps/studio/`** | React + TypeScript + Vite | **The Living Studio** SPA and Tauri 2 desktop shell. The copilot renders **agent-composed surfaces inline** — scored outcomes, opportunity theses, bet simulations — from a closed catalog the SPA owns. A feature-flagged **four-step first-run tour** starts from the PM's ambition, and a local memory records what matters across sessions. | | **`infra/cloudflare/`** | Worker | Free-plan Workers Static Assets deployment and sidecar tunnel. | | **`scripts/`** | — | Dev launcher, binary build, installer tests. | | **`tests/contract/`** | — | Cross-package MCP contract tests. | See [Architecture](docs/architecture/README.md) for the dependency graph, data flow, and testing strategy. ## Quick Start **Prerequisites:** Python 3.10+ and the [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) package manager. ```bash # Install the entire workspace (all five Python projects plus dev tooling) uv sync --all-packages # Build the Studio SPA, then launch the MCP server and Living Studio together npm --prefix apps/studio run build python scripts/dev.py ``` | Service | URL | |---|---| | MCP Server | http://localhost:8000/mcp | | The Living Studio | http://127.0.0.1:8100 | For hot reload, `npm --prefix apps/studio run dev:full` starts the MCP server, the sidecar, and Vite together on http://localhost:5173. For the desktop app, use `npm --prefix apps/studio run tauri dev`. See [Running The Living Studio](docs/living-studio.md). The first time you open the Studio, the tour asks what you want to win: an opportunity you already have in mind, a priority your boss handed you, finding the next opportunity, or pressure-testing a bet. Pick one and the conversation starts there — no form, no framework speech. It still asks for your product and audience when it needs them, and everything you say is optional and skippable. After that it opens as one room: the transcript and the composer never leave the screen. Describe a job or a customer frustration, or type `/` for commands that mirror the CLI. Whatever the thread produces — scored outcomes, an opportunity thesis, a job map, customer evidence — arrives as an inline surface, and a quiet rail above the conversation opens it in a lens that docks beside the thread instead of replacing it. Capture and simulation are conversations too: tell the studio what a customer said, or what bet you are weighing, and it renders the card. Use the bell to **catch up on outcome shifts, simulations, and telemetry signals while you were away**. The studio also remembers the person, not just the canvas. As you talk it notes what matters — your role, the opportunity, business constraints, stakeholders, evidence, how you like to work — and shows each note under **What I know** so you can confirm, correct, add, or forget it. The thread and those notes resume on the next launch. Memory lives in `~/.agentic-odi/studio.db` (override with `AGENTIC_ODI_STUDIO_DB`, or use `:memory:` for tests) and never blocks a reply if it fails. **Forget everything** clears the notes and the thread. The Studio is better with an OpenAI-compatible LLM with tool-calling support (see the [Local LLM Backend](docs/local-llm.md)), but it does not depend on one: with no model reachable it says so and every job, step, and outcome remains editable by hand. ### Connectors (MCP ↔ Living Studio) Register MCP or REST connectors that the copilot can discover and invoke. - **Where they live**: a shared `connectors.json` registry. Override its location with `AGENTIC_ODI_CONNECTORS_CONFIG`; by default it is `~/.config/agentic-odi/connectors.json`. See [External Connectors](docs/connectors.md). - **In the Living Studio**: open the **Settings** drawer → **Connectors** to list, remove, or add one of the recommended presets (Notion, PostHog, Exa, Linear, GitHub). - **Conversationally**: tell the copilot "use Notion" / "add the GitHub connector". It emits an `add_connector` local tool (handled in-process) that writes the preset to the registry, plus a `connector` SSE event the Studio surfaces as a suggestion chip. Dismissing or accepting the chip also refreshes the list. - **API**: `GET/POST/DELETE /api/connectors`, `GET /api/connectors/catalog`, and `GET /api/connectors/{name}/health` (the catalog honors `?area=` and `?recommended=true`). - **CLI**: `agentic-odi connectors catalog | add | list | health | ingest `. ### CLI at a glance The CLI is local-first, so data commands work without a running server: ```bash python -m agentic_odi_cli --version # print the Agentic ODI version python -m agentic_odi_cli --help # show available options and commands python -m agentic_odi_cli # start interactive chat in a terminal agentic-odi jobs list # Jobs-to-be-Done agentic-odi steps list --job-id agentic-odi desired-outcomes list --job-id agentic-odi customer-outcomes list agentic-odi evidence list --job-id agentic-odi schema # canonical JSON schema for every entity agentic-odi score 8 2 # ODI opportunity score → 14.00 ``` Add `--backend mcp` to route data commands through a running MCP server (`python -m agentic_odi_mcp_server`). See the [CLI Reference](docs/cli.md). ### Install the binary Prebuilt binaries are available for Linux, macOS, and Windows: ```bash curl -fsSL https://github.com/alehar9320/agentic-odi/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh ``` The installer symlinks `odi`, `odipm`, `odi-cli`, and `agentic-odi` into `~/.local/bin/`. See [Installation](docs/installation.md) for the install layout, updates, and release automation. ## Documentation | Guide | Contents | |---|---| | [CLI Reference](docs/cli.md) | Backends, interactive chat, Jobs/Steps/desired Outcomes/Customer Outcomes/evidence, `connectors`, scoring, environment variables | | [External Connectors](docs/connectors.md) | The MCP ingest connector, presets, and the `Connector` protocol | | [Running The Living Studio](docs/living-studio.md) | First-run tour and its flag, local memory and conversation resume, interface, rich inline responses and the UI catalog, run modes, desktop signing and updates, agent-driven testing (`/dev`, `/test`) | | [Local LLM Backend](docs/local-llm.md) | Running a local OpenAI-compatible model with tool calling | | [Development](docs/development.md) | Lint, format, type checks, frontend checks, tests and the coverage map | | [Architecture](docs/architecture/README.md) | Workspace layout, dependency direction, data flow, and testing | | [Installation](docs/installation.md) | Binary install, updater behavior, and release automation | | [Deployment](docs/deployment.md) | Project site on GitHub Pages, Hosted Studio and PR preview URLs, the MCP server endpoint, and the free-plan Cloudflare Worker | | [Roadmap](docs/roadmap.md) | Completed and upcoming milestones | | [Superpowers](docs/superpowers.md) | Pi, OpenCode, and Freebuff integration | Every guide above is also published on the [project site](https://alehar9320.github.io/agentic-odi/docs/), rendered from these files. The site adds a quick start, a generated MCP tool reference, and the connector catalog. ## Contributing Contributions are welcome! This project uses [Ruff](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/) for linting and formatting and [pytest](https://pytest.org/) for tests. Make sure your change passes the [lint, format, and test checks](docs/development.md) before opening a pull request. ## 🦦 Brand Odi the Otter is the mascot of Agentic ODI — a golden-ratio-derived pixel otter who appears in the CLI, the Living Studio, the desktop app icon, the favicon, and this page. The artwork is original, generated by a committed script, and documented in [brand/README.md](brand/README.md). ```bash uv run python brand/tools/render.py # regenerate every Odi asset ``` ## License This project is licensed under the terms of the MIT License — see [LICENSE](LICENSE) for details. ---
*Let's build AI that builds what people actually need.*

<content>
1: # Installation
2: 
3: Prebuilt binaries are available for Linux, macOS, and Windows. Install the latest
4: release with one command:
5: 
6: ```bash
7: curl -fsSL https://github.com/alehar9320/agentic-odi/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh
8: ```
9: 
10: The installer places the binary under `~/.local/share/agentic-odi/versions/<version>/`,
11: creates a `current` symlink, and symlinks `odi`, `odipm`, `odi-cli`, and
12: `agentic-odi` into `~/.local/bin/`.
13: 
14: If `~/.local/bin` is not on your PATH, add it (e.g.,
15: `export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"`). On Windows, the PowerShell installer
16: uses `~\AppData\Local\agentic-odi\` and copies `.exe` files to
17: `~\AppData\Local\agentic-odi\bin\`.
18: 
19: ## Update
20: 
21: By default, `odi` auto-checks for updates once every 24 hours and applies the
22: update on the next run (auto-update is enabled by default). Control behavior
23: with:
24: 
25: - `odi update` — explicit check and update
26: - `--no-update` flag — skip auto-update for this run
27: - `AGENTIC_ODI_NO_UPDATE=1` — disable auto-update globally
28: 
29: When running from a non-frozen source install, auto-update is suppressed
30: automatically.
31: 
32: ## Install layout
33: 
34: ```text
35: ~/.local/share/agentic-odi/
36:   ├── versions/<version>/
37:   │   └── odi (and bundled files)
38:   └── current -> versions/<version>
39: 
40: ~/.local/bin/
41:   ├── odi -> ../share/agentic-odi/current/odi
42:   ├── odipm
43:   ├── odi-cli
44:   └── agentic-odi
45: 
46: ~/.config/agentic-odi/  # state/preferences
47: ```
48: 
49: Environment variables: `AGENTIC_ODI_INSTALL_DIR` (override install root),
50: `XDG_DATA_HOME`, `XDG_BIN_HOME`. The default backend is `local`
51: (`--backend local`); no MCP server is required.
52: 
53: ## Unsigned binaries
54: 
55: macOS may quarantine downloaded binaries:
56: `xattr -d com.apple.quarantine ~/.local/bin/odi` (if needed). Windows SmartScreen
57: may show a warning for unsigned binaries; choose "More info → Run anyway" if you
58: trust the release.
59: 
60: ## Release automation
61: 
62: Releases are cut and published by CI with no approval step:
63: 
64: 1. Conventional commits land on `main`; `release-please` opens or updates the
65:    release PR.
66: 2. The `release-please` workflow arms auto-merge on that PR. `main` requires the
67:    `CI green` check (ruleset `main-requires-ci-green`), so the PR merges itself
68:    as soon as CI passes — nobody clicks merge.
69: 3. The merge cuts tag `vX.Y.Z` and the GitHub Release; the tag starts the
70:    `release` and `Tauri Release` workflows, which attach the CLI archives,
71:    `checksums.txt`, the install scripts, and the desktop bundles to it.
72:    The `release-instructions` job then appends an end-user "## 📦 Download &
73:    Run" section to the release page, listing the per-platform archives,
74:    `checksums.txt`, and the install scripts, plus one-line install and
75:    quick-run commands (idempotent on re-runs).
76: 4. `e2e-install` runs after `release` succeeds and installs the published binary
77:    on Linux, macOS, and Windows.
78: 
79: **One-time setup (GitHub App).** GitHub holds workflow runs that start from
80: `GITHUB_TOKEN`-authored pushes ("This workflow requires approval from a
81: maintainer") and ignores the tag such a push creates, which is why releases used
82: to need a maintainer. A release-only GitHub App avoids both:
83: 
84: 1. Settings → Developer settings → GitHub Apps → New GitHub App, with
85:    permissions: Contents `Read and write`, Issues `Read and write`, Pull
86:    requests `Read and write` (no webhook).
87: 2. Install the App on this repository.
88: 3. Add repository secrets `RELEASE_PLEASE_APP_CLIENT_ID` (the App's client ID)
89:    and `RELEASE_PLEASE_APP_PRIVATE_KEY` (a generated private key).
90: 
91: Until those secrets exist, the `release-please` workflow logs a warning and falls
92: back to `GITHUB_TOKEN`: releases still happen, but the release PR needs a
93: maintainer approval and merge, and the tag will not start the asset builds. After
94: adding the secrets, re-run the workflow (`gh workflow run release-please.yml`) or
95: push to `main` so the open release PR is re-driven by the App.
96: 
97: To check the installer without cutting a release, run
98: `bash scripts/tests/install_e2e.sh` — it serves a simulated release over HTTP and
99: exercises `scripts/install.sh` end to end (CI runs it too).

(End of file - total 99 lines)
</content>

If `~/.local/bin` is not on your PATH, add it (e.g.,
`export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"`). On Windows, the PowerShell installer
uses `~\AppData\Local\agentic-odi\` and copies `.exe` files to
`~\AppData\Local\agentic-odi\bin\`.

## Update

By default, `odi` auto-checks for updates once every 24 hours and applies the
update on the next run (auto-update is enabled by default). Control behavior
with:

- `odi update` — explicit check and update
- `--no-update` flag — skip auto-update for this run
- `AGENTIC_ODI_NO_UPDATE=1` — disable auto-update globally

When running from a non-frozen source install, auto-update is suppressed
automatically.

## Install layout

```text
~/.local/share/agentic-odi/
  ├── versions/<version>/
  │   └── odi (and bundled files)
  └── current -> versions/<version>

~/.local/bin/
  ├── odi -> ../share/agentic-odi/current/odi
  ├── odipm
  ├── odi-cli
  └── agentic-odi

~/.config/agentic-odi/  # state/preferences
```

Environment variables: `AGENTIC_ODI_INSTALL_DIR` (override install root),
`XDG_DATA_HOME`, `XDG_BIN_HOME`. The default backend is `local`
(`--backend local`); no MCP server is required.

## Unsigned binaries

macOS may quarantine downloaded binaries:
`xattr -d com.apple.quarantine ~/.local/bin/odi` (if needed). Windows SmartScreen
may show a warning for unsigned binaries; choose "More info → Run anyway" if you
trust the release.

## Release automation

Releases are cut and published by CI with no approval step:

1. Conventional commits land on `main`; `release-please` opens or updates the
   release PR.
2. The `release-please` workflow arms auto-merge on that PR. `main` requires the
   `CI green` check (ruleset `main-requires-ci-green`), so the PR merges itself
   as soon as CI passes — nobody clicks merge.
3. The merge cuts tag `vX.Y.Z` and the GitHub Release; the tag starts the
   `release` and `Tauri Release` workflows, which attach the CLI archives,
   `checksums.txt`, the install scripts, and the desktop bundles to it.
   The `release-instructions` job then appends an end-user "## 📦 Download &
   Run" section to the release page, listing the per-platform archives,
   `checksums.txt`, and the install scripts, plus one-line install and
   quick-run commands (idempotent on re-runs).
4. `e2e-install` runs after `release` succeeds and installs the published binary
   on Linux, macOS, and Windows.

**One-time setup (GitHub App).** GitHub holds workflow runs that start from
`GITHUB_TOKEN`-authored pushes ("This workflow requires approval from a
maintainer") and ignores the tag such a push creates, which is why releases used
to need a maintainer. A release-only GitHub App avoids both:

1. Settings → Developer settings → GitHub Apps → New GitHub App, with
   permissions: Contents `Read and write`, Issues `Read and write`, Pull
   requests `Read and write` (no webhook).
2. Install the App on this repository.
3. Add repository secrets `RELEASE_PLEASE_APP_CLIENT_ID` (the App's client ID)
   and `RELEASE_PLEASE_APP_PRIVATE_KEY` (a generated private key).

Until those secrets exist, the `release-please` workflow logs a warning and falls
back to `GITHUB_TOKEN`: releases still happen, but the release PR needs a
maintainer approval and merge, and the tag will not start the asset builds. After
adding the secrets, re-run the workflow (`gh workflow run release-please.yml`) or
push to `main` so the open release PR is re-driven by the App.

To check the installer without cutting a release, run
`bash scripts/tests/install_e2e.sh` — it serves a simulated release over HTTP and
exercises `scripts/install.sh` end to end (CI runs it too).

# Deployment

## Project Site (GitHub Pages)

The static site in `website/` is published to
**[https://alehar9320.github.io/agentic-odi/](https://alehar9320.github.io/agentic-odi/)**
by [`.github/workflows/pages.yml`](../.github/workflows/pages.yml).

- A push to `main` runs the website tests, builds `_site` from `website/`, and
  deploys the artifact with `actions/deploy-pages`.
- `workflow_dispatch` republishes the site from the Actions tab without a code
  change.
- Pages is configured with the "GitHub Actions" source, so there is no
  `gh-pages` branch. Removing `pages.yml` stops all publishing and the site
  returns 404.
- The `github-pages` environment only allows deployments from `main`.

## Hosted MCP Server

The server is deployed via **[Horizon Prefect](https://www.prefect.io/horizon)**,
Prefect's managed infrastructure for hosting MCP-compatible agents.

## Test Chat (UI)

Interact with the deployed agent directly in your browser:

> **[https://horizon.prefect.io/alhase/servers/agentic-odi/chat](https://horizon.prefect.io/alhase/servers/agentic-odi/chat)**

## MCP Server Endpoint

Integrate via the MCP protocol at:

> **[https://agentic-odi.fastmcp.app/mcp](https://agentic-odi.fastmcp.app/mcp)**

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Authentication is required** to access the MCP server endpoint. Please reach
> out to the maintainers to obtain the necessary credentials before connecting a
> client.

## Hosted Studio

The Living Studio SPA is deployed to Cloudflare Workers:

| Environment | URL |
|---|---|
| Production (`main`) | **[https://agentic-odi.alehar.workers.dev/](https://agentic-odi.alehar.workers.dev/)** |
| Pull request preview | Posted automatically by Cloudflare Workers Builds as a PR comment |

Production deploys on every push to `main`. The Worker is `agentic-odi`; keep
`name` in `wrangler.jsonc` aligned with the Worker connected in the dashboard.
Preview builds run for non-production branches and are ephemeral: the Cloudflare
PR comment is the source of truth, so do not copy a preview URL into docs. The
hosted UI loads without a backend; canvas data, chat, and mutations need the
sidecar tunnel described below.

## Living Studio on a Free Cloudflare Worker

Workers Containers — the only way to run the Python sidecar entirely on
Cloudflare — requires the Workers Paid plan. On the free plan, the Worker serves
the built SPA as Workers Static Assets and proxies `/api/*` to the sidecar
through a free, account-less
[Cloudflare Quick Tunnel](https://developers.cloudflare.com/tunnel/get-started/quick-tunnels/).

`wrangler.jsonc` publishes `apps/studio/dist` with SPA fallback and runs the Worker
first for `/api/*`; `infra/cloudflare/worker.ts` forwards those calls to the
`SIDECAR_URL` secret. The browser only talks to the Worker origin, so the
sidecar's CORS list is not involved.

```bash
# 1. Build the SPA that the Worker uploads as static assets
npm --prefix apps/studio ci
npm --prefix apps/studio run build

# 2. Terminal A — MCP server (:8000) + sidecar (:8100)
python scripts/dev.py

# 3. Terminal B — free public URL for the sidecar (no account required)
cloudflared tunnel --url http://127.0.0.1:8100
# copy the https://<random>.trycloudflare.com URL it prints

# 4. Store the URL on the Worker, then deploy
npx wrangler secret put SIDECAR_URL   # paste the trycloudflare URL
npx wrangler deploy
```

Workers Builds settings (Workers & Pages → your Worker → Settings → Builds):

| Setting | Value |
|---|---|
| Production branch | `main` |
| Root directory | `/` |
| Build command | `npm --prefix apps/studio ci && npm --prefix apps/studio run build` |
| Deploy command | `npx wrangler deploy` |
| Preview command | `npx wrangler preview` |

A Worker has no run command: the Worker script runs on Cloudflare. Set `name` in
`wrangler.jsonc` to the Worker you created before the first deploy.

### Pull request previews

Workers Builds posts the build status and Preview URL to the pull request
automatically. To enable it:

1. Open the Worker → **Settings** → **Build** → **Branch control**.
2. Keep the production branch set to `main` and enable **Preview Builds**.
3. If Cloudflare shows **Set up Worker Previews**, complete the one-time switch.
   This cannot be reversed.
4. Confirm the Preview command is `npx wrangler preview`.

`wrangler.jsonc` must keep a `previews` block, even an empty one: the
`wrangler preview` command fails the build with "Your Wrangler configuration is
missing a `previews` block" without it. Assets and compatibility settings stay
at the top level, so `"previews": {}` is enough while Previews need no extra
settings. If a future Preview needs vars or bindings, add them under `previews`
with Preview-safe values.

Previews do not inherit production settings. The SPA loads from a Preview, but
`/api/*` returns `502 SIDECAR_URL is not configured` until a preview-specific
`SIDECAR_URL` secret is configured:

```bash
npx wrangler preview secret put SIDECAR_URL --name <branch>
```

When `--name` is omitted it defaults to the current git branch. Previews are
ephemeral, and pull requests from forks may not receive one. If Cloudflare does
not comment, paste the URL into the PR's **Deployment** section.

The `cf` CLI can inspect build triggers and recent builds (`cf builds triggers
list`, `cf builds list`) and create a Preview (`cf previews deploy`), but it does
not post GitHub PR comments. The Workers Builds Git integration owns the PR link;
`cf` is only an optional verification tool and requires `cf auth login`.

> [!NOTE]
> The sidecar runs on your machine, so the Worker only works while
> `python scripts/dev.py` and the Quick Tunnel are running. Quick Tunnel URLs
> change on every restart — update the secret with
> `npx wrangler secret put SIDECAR_URL`. Chat also needs a reachable
> OpenAI-compatible endpoint in the Studio's **Settings**; the canvas, job map,
> and impact simulation work without one.

1: # Development
2: 
3: Everything below mirrors what CI runs. Install the workspace first:
4: 
5: ```bash
6: uv sync --all-packages
7: ```
8: 
9: ## Linting, Formatting & Type Checks
10: 
11: Shared tooling lives in the root `pyproject.toml`, so one command covers every
12: Python project:
13: 
14: ```bash
15: uv run ruff check .
16: uv run ruff format --check .
17: uv run mypy apps packages
18: uv run --directory website mypy .
19: 
20: # Security scanning
21: uv run bandit -c pyproject.toml -r apps packages website/
22: ```
23: 
24: ## Frontend & Desktop Checks (studio)
25: 
26: The SPA and Tauri shell mirror their CI jobs locally:
27: 
28: ```bash
29: npm --prefix apps/studio run lint       # ESLint
30: npm --prefix apps/studio run typecheck  # tsc --noEmit
31: npm --prefix apps/studio test -- --run  # Vitest (run once)
32: npm --prefix apps/studio run build      # production build → apps/studio/dist
33: cd apps/studio/src-tauri && cargo fmt --check && cargo clippy -- -D warnings && cargo check
34: ```
35: 
36: ### Conversational UI coverage
37: 
38: The agent-composed surfaces and the first-run tour are covered at these levels:
39: 
40: | File | What it covers |
41: |---|---|
42: | `apps/studio/src/ui/protocol.test.ts` | Spec parsing: prop types, enums, ranges, required props, depth/node/size ceilings, unknown types |
43: | `apps/studio/src/ui/UiRenderer.test.tsx` | Card rendering, computed opportunity scores, action dispatch, per-node failure isolation, catalog/registry parity |
44: | `apps/studio/src/components/chat/Conversation.test.tsx` | Prose and surfaces interleaved in the agent's order; card actions become messages |
45: | `apps/studio-api/tests/test_studio_ui_spec.py` | Catalog validation and `render_ui` tool-schema generation |
46: | `apps/studio-api/tests/test_studio_chat_ui.py` | `render_ui` interception, `ui` SSE events, and the correction fed back to the model |
47: | `apps/studio/src/features/flags.test.ts` | Flag precedence (query → storage → env → default), value parsing, local overrides |
48: | `apps/studio/src/onboarding/machine.test.ts` | Tour transitions, no forward motion without a goal, versioned storage, malformed records |
49: | `apps/studio/src/onboarding/FirstRunWizard.test.tsx` | Auto-open, full flow to a destination, skip/Escape, focus trap, resume, replay, inline model repair, flag off |
50: | `apps/studio/src/App.test.tsx` | First-run ordering: tour over the context conversation, job handoff, chosen surface opens, flag off in shell tests |
51: 
52: ## Website Checks (GitHub Pages)
53: 
54: The `website/` static site is part of the main CI workflow. Its tests assert the
55: committed OG art is reproducible, that `index.html` stays in sync with the
56: README, and that the publish pipeline (`website/tests/test_pages_deploy.py`)
57: still exists:
58: 
59: ```bash
60: uv run --directory website pytest tests/
61: ```
62: 
63: Publishing happens in `.github/workflows/pages.yml`: it runs those tests, builds
64: `_site` from `website/`, and deploys the artifact with `actions/deploy-pages` on
65: every push to `main`. There is no `gh-pages` branch, so that workflow is the only
66: thing that keeps <https://alehar9320.github.io/agentic-odi/> online.
67: 
68: ## Formatting workflow
69: 
70: - **When editing Python files**, either rely on the **pre-commit hooks** below
71:   (recommended) or run Ruff formatting directly before pushing:
72: 
73:   ```bash
74:   uv run ruff format .
75:   ```
76: 
77: - **CI behavior**:
78:   - CI runs `uv run ruff check .` to lint without modifying files.
79:   - CI runs `uv run ruff format --check .` to *verify* formatting only.
80:   - If CI fails on formatting, run `uv run ruff format .` locally, commit the
81:     changes, and push again.
82: 
83: ## Pre-commit hooks
84: 
85: To run the checks automatically before each commit:
86: 
87: ```bash
88: uv tool install pre-commit
89: pre-commit install
90: ```
91: 
92: After this, `ruff` and `ruff-format` run on staged files whenever you commit.
93: You can also trigger them manually:
94: 
95: ```bash
96: pre-commit run --all-files
97: ```
98: 
99: ## Testing
100: 
101: Tests use **pytest** with **pytest-asyncio** (strict mode) and run entirely
102: in-memory — no running server required. Tests live next to the package they
103: cover, and every test runs from the repository root:
104: 
105: ```bash
106: uv run pytest                        # everything
107: uv run pytest apps/cli               # one app
108: uv run pytest packages/core          # one package
109: uv run pytest tests/contract         # cross-package contracts
110: uv run pytest tests/scripts          # dev launcher
111: ```
112: 
113: The MCP server contract test compares the live FastMCP registry with
114: `packages/core/src/agentic_odi_core/contract.py`, so add or change a tool in
115: both places. The CLI local-backend contract test keeps `_LOCAL_HANDLERS` aligned
116: with the same tool names.
117: 
118: ## Test Coverage
119: 
120: CI runs the suite on Python **3.10, 3.11, and 3.12** and uploads one combined
121: `coverage.xml` from the 3.12 job to
122: [Codecov](https://codecov.io/gh/alehar9320/agentic-odi).
123: 
124: The Codecov upload authenticates with the `CODECOV_TOKEN` repository secret and
125: is non-blocking (`fail_ci_if_error: false`), so a Codecov outage or a fork PR
126: without secrets cannot fail the test job. The badge at the top of the README
127: tracks `main`, which is the baseline every PR is compared against:
128: 
129: - **Project** status requires at least **90%** coverage (`target: 90%`) and
130:   tolerates a 1% dip from `codecov.yml`.
131: - **Patch** status is informational for now, so new code can land while the
132:   suite catches up.
133: 
134: To reproduce the report locally:
135: 
136: ```bash
137: uv run pytest \
138:   --cov=agentic_odi_cli \
139:   --cov=agentic_odi_connectors \
140:   --cov=agentic_odi_core \
141:   --cov=agentic_odi_mcp_server \
142:   --cov=agentic_odi_studio_api \
143:   --cov-report=term-missing \
144:   --cov-report=xml:coverage.xml
145: ```
146: 
147: > [!NOTE]
148: > Coverage is only collected for the Python packages. `apps/studio/` and test
149: > directories are excluded in `codecov.yml`.
150: 
151: ### Conventions
152: 
153: - Test files live under each project's `tests/` directory and are named
154:   `test_*.py`.
155: - Root `tests/` is reserved for cross-package checks (`contract/` and
156:   `scripts/`).
157: - Every async test is decorated with `@pytest.mark.asyncio`.
158: - Use `Client(mcp)` directly (no HTTP server needed) for fast, isolated tests.
159: - The MCP server's `reset_db` autouse fixture clears in-memory state before
160:   each test.
161: 
162: ### Test Coverage Map
163: 
164: | Area | What it covers |
165: |---|---|
166: | `packages/core/tests/` | Domain models, opportunity scoring, `ODIService`, repository implementations, SQLite persistence, schema, and repository factory |
167: | `apps/mcp-server/tests/` | Full ODI workflow, entity parity, context tools, Customer Outcomes, evidence, tool errors, and HTTP transport startup |
168: | `apps/studio-api/tests/` | Health, config, canvas, SSE chat, SPA fallback, MCP hydration, probes, and step/outcome passthrough |
169: | `apps/cli/tests/` | Backend selection, local/remote CRUD, chat, wizard, onboarding, updates, rendering, connectors, and startup performance |
170: | `packages/connectors/tests/` | Catalog presets, registry persistence, factory, MCP and REST connectors, evidence mapping, and sink |
171: | `tests/contract/` | Live MCP tool surface and CLI local-handler parity |
172: | `tests/scripts/` | `scripts/dev.py` startup, port checks, signals, and shutdown |
173: | `apps/studio/src/**/*.test.ts` | SPA units: ODI math, transport bridge, SSE parser, sidecar client |
174: | `website/tests/` | Static site integrity, OG art reproducibility, and README sync |
175: 
176: > [!TIP]
177: > Type `/test` in the AI assistant to have the agent run all tests and report the
178: > results automatically.
179:

# Development

Everything below mirrors what CI runs. Install the workspace first:

```bash
uv sync --all-packages
```

## Linting, Formatting & Type Checks

Shared tooling lives in the root `pyproject.toml`, so one command covers every
Python project:

```bash
uv run ruff check .
uv run ruff format --check .
uv run mypy apps packages
uv run --directory website mypy .

# Security scanning
uv run bandit -c pyproject.toml -r apps packages website/
```

## Frontend & Desktop Checks (studio)

The SPA and Tauri shell mirror their CI jobs locally:

```bash
npm --prefix apps/studio run lint       # ESLint
npm --prefix apps/studio run typecheck  # tsc --noEmit
npm --prefix apps/studio test -- --run  # Vitest (run once)
npm --prefix apps/studio run build      # production build → apps/studio/dist
cd apps/studio/src-tauri && cargo fmt --check && cargo clippy -- -D warnings && cargo check
```

### Conversational UI coverage

The agent-composed surfaces and the first-run tour are covered at these levels:

| File | What it covers |
|---|---|
| `apps/studio/src/ui/protocol.test.ts` | Spec parsing: prop types, enums, ranges, required props, depth/node/size ceilings, unknown types |
| `apps/studio/src/ui/UiRenderer.test.tsx` | Card rendering, computed opportunity scores, action dispatch, per-node failure isolation, catalog/registry parity |
| `apps/studio/src/components/chat/Conversation.test.tsx` | Prose and surfaces interleaved in the agent's order; card actions become messages |
| `apps/studio-api/tests/test_studio_ui_spec.py` | Catalog validation and `render_ui` tool-schema generation |
| `apps/studio-api/tests/test_studio_chat_ui.py` | `render_ui` interception, `ui` SSE events, and the correction fed back to the model |
| `apps/studio/src/features/flags.test.ts` | Flag precedence (query → storage → env → default), value parsing, local overrides |
| `apps/studio/src/onboarding/machine.test.ts` | Tour transitions, no forward motion without a goal, versioned storage, malformed records |
| `apps/studio/src/onboarding/FirstRunWizard.test.tsx` | Auto-open, full flow to a destination, skip/Escape, focus trap, resume, replay, inline model repair, flag off |
| `apps/studio/src/App.test.tsx` | First-run ordering: tour over the context conversation, job handoff, chosen surface opens, flag off in shell tests |

## Website Checks (GitHub Pages)

The `website/` static site is part of the main CI workflow. Its tests assert the
committed OG art is reproducible, that `index.html` stays in sync with the
README, and that the publish pipeline (`website/tests/test_pages_deploy.py`)
still exists:

```bash
uv run --directory website pytest tests/
```

Publishing happens in `.github/workflows/pages.yml`: it runs those tests, builds
`_site` from `website/`, and deploys the artifact with `actions/deploy-pages` on
every push to `main`. There is no `gh-pages` branch, so that workflow is the only
thing that keeps <https://alehar9320.github.io/agentic-odi/> online.

## Formatting workflow

- **When editing Python files**, either rely on the **pre-commit hooks** below
  (recommended) or run Ruff formatting directly before pushing:

  ```bash
  uv run ruff format .
  ```

- **CI behavior**:
  - CI runs `uv run ruff check .` to lint without modifying files.
  - CI runs `uv run ruff format --check .` to *verify* formatting only.
  - If CI fails on formatting, run `uv run ruff format .` locally, commit the
    changes, and push again.

## Pre-commit hooks

To run the checks automatically before each commit:

```bash
uv tool install pre-commit
pre-commit install
```

After this, `ruff` and `ruff-format` run on staged files whenever you commit.
You can also trigger them manually:

```bash
pre-commit run --all-files
```

## Testing

Tests use **pytest** with **pytest-asyncio** (strict mode) and run entirely
in-memory — no running server required. Tests live next to the package they
cover, and every test runs from the repository root:

```bash
uv run pytest                        # everything
uv run pytest apps/cli               # one app
uv run pytest packages/core          # one package
uv run pytest tests/contract         # cross-package contracts
uv run pytest tests/scripts          # dev launcher
```

The MCP server contract test compares the live FastMCP registry with
`packages/core/src/agentic_odi_core/contract.py`, so add or change a tool in
both places. The CLI local-backend contract test keeps `_LOCAL_HANDLERS` aligned
with the same tool names.

## Test Coverage

CI runs the suite on Python **3.10, 3.11, and 3.12** and uploads one combined
`coverage.xml` from the 3.12 job to
[Codecov](https://codecov.io/gh/alehar9320/agentic-odi).

The Codecov upload authenticates with the `CODECOV_TOKEN` repository secret and
is non-blocking (`fail_ci_if_error: false`), so a Codecov outage or a fork PR
without secrets cannot fail the test job. The badge at the top of the README
tracks `main`, which is the baseline every PR is compared against:

- **Project** status requires at least **90%** coverage (`target: 90%`) and
  tolerates a 1% dip from `codecov.yml`.
- **Patch** status is informational for now, so new code can land while the
  suite catches up.

To reproduce the report locally:

```bash
uv run pytest \
  --cov=agentic_odi_cli \
  --cov=agentic_odi_connectors \
  --cov=agentic_odi_core \
  --cov=agentic_odi_mcp_server \
  --cov=agentic_odi_studio_api \
  --cov-report=term-missing \
  --cov-report=xml:coverage.xml
```

> [!NOTE]
> Coverage is only collected for the Python packages. `apps/studio/` and test
> directories are excluded in `codecov.yml`.

### Conventions

- Test files live under each project's `tests/` directory and are named
  `test_*.py`.
- Root `tests/` is reserved for cross-package checks (`contract/` and
  `scripts/`).
- Every async test is decorated with `@pytest.mark.asyncio`.
- Use `Client(mcp)` directly (no HTTP server needed) for fast, isolated tests.
- The MCP server's `reset_db` autouse fixture clears in-memory state before
  each test.

### Test Coverage Map

| Area | What it covers |
|---|---|
| `packages/core/tests/` | Domain models, opportunity scoring, `ODIService`, repository implementations, SQLite persistence, schema, and repository factory |
| `apps/mcp-server/tests/` | Full ODI workflow, entity parity, context tools, Customer Outcomes, evidence, tool errors, and HTTP transport startup |
| `apps/studio-api/tests/` | Health, config, canvas, SSE chat, SPA fallback, MCP hydration, probes, and step/outcome passthrough |
| `apps/cli/tests/` | Backend selection, local/remote CRUD, chat, wizard, onboarding, updates, rendering, connectors, and startup performance |
| `packages/connectors/tests/` | Catalog presets, registry persistence, factory, MCP and REST connectors, evidence mapping, and sink |
| `tests/contract/` | Live MCP tool surface and CLI local-handler parity |
| `tests/scripts/` | `scripts/dev.py` startup, port checks, signals, and shutdown |
| `apps/studio/src/**/*.test.ts` | SPA units: ODI math, transport bridge, SSE parser, sidecar client |
| `website/tests/` | Static site integrity, OG art reproducibility, and README sync |

> [!TIP]
> Type `/test` in the AI assistant to have the agent run all tests and report the
> results automatically.

## Agent Session Tracking

Agent sessions are captured with the [Entire](https://docs.entire.io/overview)
CLI. The repository integration lives in `.entire/settings.json`,
`.cursor/hooks.json`, and `.opencode/plugins/entire.ts`. Run `entire status` to
confirm it is enabled and `entire checkpoint list` to inspect captured
checkpoints.

  security:

      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        python-version: ["3.10", "3.11", "3.12"]

          token: ${{ secrets.CODECOV_TOKEN }}
          files: coverage.xml
          fail_ci_if_error: false

  smoke:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    needs: [lint, typecheck, security, test]
    timeout-minutes: 15
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: ./.github/actions/setup

      - name: CLI reports a version
        run: |
          version="$(uv run python -m agentic_odi_cli --version)"
          [ -n "$version" ]
          echo "OK: $version"

      - name: CLI exposes connectors commands
        run: |
          help="$(uv run python -m agentic_odi_cli connectors --help)"
          echo "$help" | grep -q list
          echo "$help" | grep -q ingest
          echo "OK: connectors help"

      - name: Installer installs from a simulated release
        run: bash scripts/tests/install_e2e.sh

      - name: MCP server boots and serves /mcp
        run: |
          uv run python -m agentic_odi_mcp_server > /tmp/mcp_server.log 2>&1 &
          SERVER_PID=$!
          probe() {
            curl -sfX POST http://localhost:8000/mcp \
              -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
              -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"initialize","id":1,"params":{"protocolVersion":"2024-11-05","capabilities":{},"clientInfo":{"name":"ci","version":"1"}}}' \
              -o /dev/null
          }
          ok=0
          for _ in $(seq 1 30); do
            if probe; then ok=1; break; fi
            sleep 1
          done
          kill "$SERVER_PID" 2>/dev/null || true
          wait "$SERVER_PID" 2>/dev/null || true
          if [ "$ok" -ne 1 ]; then
            echo "MCP server did not respond on :8000/mcp"
            cat /tmp/mcp_server.log
            exit 1
          fi
          echo "OK: MCP server responded with 200"

      - name: Living Studio sidecar serves the studio API
        run: |
          AGENTIC_ODI_BACKEND=mcp uv run python -m agentic_odi_studio_api.main > /tmp/sidecar.log 2>&1 &
          SIDECAR_PID=$!
          probe() {
            curl -fsS -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8100/api/health/mcp \
              -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
              -d '{"mcp_url":"http://127.0.0.1:8000/mcp"}' -o /dev/null &&
              curl -fsS "http://127.0.0.1:8100/api/canvas?mcp_url=http://127.0.0.1:8000/mcp" -o /dev/null
          }
          ok=0
          for _ in $(seq 1 30); do
            if probe; then ok=1; break; fi
            sleep 1
          done
          kill "$SIDECAR_PID" 2>/dev/null || true
          wait "$SIDECAR_PID" 2>/dev/null || true
          if [ "$ok" -ne 1 ]; then
            echo "Living Studio sidecar did not respond on :8100"
            cat /tmp/sidecar.log
            exit 1
          fi
          echo "OK: sidecar studio API responded with 200"

      - name: scripts/dev.py brings up both services and stops cleanly
        run: |
          uv run python scripts/dev.py > /tmp/clientrun.log 2>&1 &
          RUN_PID=$!
          probe() {
            curl -sf -o /dev/null http://127.0.0.1:8100/api/config &&
              curl -sfX POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/mcp \
                -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
                -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"initialize","id":1,"params":{"protocolVersion":"2024-11-05","capabilities":{},"clientInfo":{"name":"ci","version":"1"}}}' \
                -o /dev/null
          }
          ok=0
          for _ in $(seq 1 60); do
            if probe; then ok=1; break; fi
            sleep 1
          done
          if [ "$ok" -ne 1 ]; then
            echo "scripts/dev.py did not bring up both services"
            cat /tmp/clientrun.log
            kill "$RUN_PID" 2>/dev/null || true
            exit 1
          fi
          kill -INT "$RUN_PID"
          wait "$RUN_PID"
          echo "OK: both services stopped cleanly"

  website:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 15
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: ./.github/actions/setup

      # The site is generated and committed so a reviewer can read the
      # rendered HTML in a pull request. If the committed copy no longer
      # matches a fresh build, the site has drifted and the PR is not ready.
      - name: Check the committed site matches a fresh build
        run: uv run python website/tools/build_site.py --check

      - name: Pytest (website)
        run: uv run --directory website pytest tests/

      - name: Build site
        run: uv run python website/tools/build_site.py --out _site

  studio:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 15
    defaults:
      run:
        shell: bash
        working-directory: apps/studio
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version: "lts/*"
          cache: npm
          cache-dependency-path: apps/studio/package-lock.json

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm ci

      - name: Lint
        run: npm run lint

      - name: Typecheck
        run: npm run typecheck

      - name: Unit tests
        run: npm test -- --run

      - name: Build
        run: npm run build

      - name: Verify generated API types are up to date
        run: |
          npm run gen:api-types
          git diff --exit-code -- src/api/schema.d.ts

  tauri-check:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 30
    defaults:
      run:
        shell: bash
        working-directory: apps/studio/src-tauri
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7

      - name: Install Linux webview dependencies
        run: |
          sudo apt-get update
          sudo apt-get install -y libwebkit2gtk-4.1-dev build-essential curl wget file \
            libxdo-dev libssl-dev libayatana-appindicator3-dev librsvg2-dev patchelf

      - uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable
        with:
          components: rustfmt, clippy

      - uses: swatinem/rust-cache@v2
        with:
          workspaces: apps/studio/src-tauri -> target

      - name: Cargo fmt
        run: cargo fmt --check

      - name: Cargo clippy
        run: cargo clippy -- -D warnings

      - name: Cargo check
        run: cargo check

  tauri-build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 60
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7

      - name: Install Linux webview dependencies
        run: |
          sudo apt-get update
          sudo apt-get install -y libwebkit2gtk-4.1-dev build-essential curl wget file \
            libxdo-dev libssl-dev libayatana-appindicator3-dev librsvg2-dev patchelf

      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version: "lts/*"
          cache: npm
          cache-dependency-path: apps/studio/package-lock.json

      - uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable

      - uses: swatinem/rust-cache@v2
        with:
          workspaces: apps/studio/src-tauri -> target

      - name: Install frontend dependencies
        run: npm ci
        working-directory: apps/studio

      # Dependabot PRs cannot read repository secrets, so the signing key is
      # empty there. Export it only when present and disable updater artifacts
      # otherwise; passing an empty key makes the bundler try (and fail) to
      # decode it.
      - name: Build desktop bundle
        working-directory: apps/studio
        env:
          SIGNING_KEY: ${{ secrets.TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY }}
          SIGNING_KEY_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY_PASSWORD }}
        run: |
          if [ -n "$SIGNING_KEY" ]; then
            export TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY="$SIGNING_KEY"
            export TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY_PASSWORD="$SIGNING_KEY_PASSWORD"
            npm run tauri -- build
          else
            echo "No TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY provided — building without signed updater artifacts."
            npm run tauri -- build --config '{"bundle":{"createUpdaterArtifacts":false}}'
          fi

      - name: Upload desktop bundles
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        with:
          name: tauri-bundles-linux
          if-no-files-found: warn
          path: |
            apps/studio/src-tauri/target/release/bundle/deb/*.deb
            apps/studio/src-tauri/target/release/bundle/appimage/*.AppImage
            apps/studio/src-tauri/target/release/bundle/appimage/*.AppImage.sig

  ci-green:
    name: CI green
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    needs: [lint, typecheck, security, test, smoke, website, studio, tauri-check, tauri-build]
    if: always()
    steps:
      - name: Verify all required jobs succeeded
        run: |
          results='${{ join(needs.*.result, ' ') }}'
          echo "Job results: $results"
          for result in $results; do
            if [ "$result" != "success" ]; then
              echo "::error::A required job did not succeed ($results)"
              exit 1
            fi
          done
          echo "OK: all required jobs succeeded"

name: release

on:
  push:
    tags:
      - "v*"

permissions:
  contents: write

jobs:
  build:
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        include:
          - os: linux
            runner: ubuntu-latest
            target: linux_x86_64
          - os: linux
            runner: ubuntu-24.04-arm
            target: linux_arm64
          - os: macos
            runner: macos-14
            target: macos_arm64
          - os: macos
            runner: macos-15-intel
            target: macos_x86_64
          - os: windows
            runner: windows-latest
            target: windows_x86_64
    # No container: the Node-based actions (checkout, setup-uv) need glibc >= 2.28,
    # which the manylinux2014 images (glibc 2.17) cannot provide. If a narrower
    # glibc floor is needed later, use a manylinux_2_28 image instead.
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.runner }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - name: Setup uv
        uses: ./.github/actions/setup
        with:
          python-version: "3.11"
      - name: Build
        env:
          TARGET: ${{ matrix.target }}
        run: |
          VERSION="${GITHUB_REF_NAME#v}"
          RELEASE_DATE_UTC="$(git log -1 --format=%cI)"
          export VERSION RELEASE_DATE_UTC
          bash scripts/build_binary.sh
      - name: Write checksums
        shell: bash
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          shopt -s nullglob
          archives=(odi_*.tar.gz odi_*.zip)
          if [ "${#archives[@]}" -eq 0 ]; then
            echo "::error::No archive was produced for ${{ matrix.target }}"
            exit 1
          fi
          if command -v sha256sum >/dev/null 2>&1; then
            sha256sum "${archives[@]}" > "checksums-${{ matrix.target }}.txt"
          elif command -v shasum >/dev/null 2>&1; then
            shasum -a 256 "${archives[@]}" > "checksums-${{ matrix.target }}.txt"
          else
            echo "::error::No sha256 tool available on ${{ matrix.runner }}"
            exit 1
          fi
          cat "checksums-${{ matrix.target }}.txt"
      - name: Upload checksums fragment
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        with:
          name: checksums-${{ matrix.target }}
          path: checksums-${{ matrix.target }}.txt
          if-no-files-found: error
      - name: Upload assets
        uses: softprops/action-gh-release@v3
        with:
          files: |
            odi_*.tar.gz
            odi_*.zip

  checksums:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v8
        with:
          pattern: checksums-*
          path: fragments
          merge-multiple: true
      - name: Combine per-target checksums
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          cat fragments/checksums-*.txt | sort -k2 > checksums.txt
          test -s checksums.txt
          echo "checksums.txt"
          cat checksums.txt
      - name: Upload checksums.txt
        uses: softprops/action-gh-release@v3
        with:
          files: checksums.txt

  upload-installers:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - name: Upload install scripts
        uses: softprops/action-gh-release@v3
        with:
          files: |
            scripts/install.sh
            scripts/install.ps1

  release-instructions:
    needs: [checksums, upload-installers]
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - name: Setup uv
        uses: ./.github/actions/setup
        with:
          python-version: "3.11"
      - name: Publish download & run instructions on the release
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
        run: |
          python scripts/release_instructions.py \
            --tag "${{ github.ref_name }}" \
            --repo "${{ github.repository }}"
